extracted.intended_audience: fiction and creative writers who want to learn deliberately from their influences
extracted.subtask_description: How-to guidance for studying works that inspire you: break them into component parts, identify what you love, practice those elements, and deliberately transform them into your own voice while avoiding plagiarism or over-influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissect the thing you love / reverse engineer
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the thing and you literally have to dissect it, cut it open and take all the little pieces out and you have to break it down into little bits and find out, okay, why do I like this as much as I do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break a work into components (plot beats, characterization, line style, lighting, staging, world rules). Reverse-engineer how effects are achieved rather than assuming how the creator worked. Example: examine why Katara's 'bloodbending' resonates — see what questions it answers about the magic system.

rubrics_metrics.name: List the specific elements you find appealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down a list of the specific elements you find appealing in a slice of something that inspires you (book, movie, art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write out concrete features in sketchbooks or notes (thin line art, implied journeys, found-family themes). The episode homework explicitly asks listeners to take a slice and list elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate themes / look for commonalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for commonalities, themes that call to you across multiple inspirations so you can identify what consistently appeals to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect examples (Pinterest boards, playlists) to reveal recurring motifs (implied journeys, camaraderie). Use the aggregated themes as a compass to intentionally pull those themes into your own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach self-correction with generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach your self corrections with a generous heart — seek to plus and improve rather than knock yourself down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be analytic without harsh self-flagellation: identify places to improve and iterate. Treat revision as additive rather than apologetic; let excitement for your work show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pull feelings from inspirations and feed them into your work
rubrics_metrics.description: Pull that feeling from your inspiration so that you can then feed it into your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of copying specifics, extract the emotional effect (excitement, sorrow, wonder) and recreate those feelings via your own characters and situations. Allow yourself to be excited about your own work like fan creators do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust your voice ('No one can do me like me')
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if elements overlap with other works, the whole of your work — your theming, staging, and voice — makes it yours: 'No one can do me like me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mantra to reduce anxiety of influence; accept shared genre conventions while focusing on your unique combination of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go adjacent to avoid direct copying
rubrics_metrics.description: If you worry consuming a specific source will make you copy it, go adjacent — find other ways to get into the same headspace without direct imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if afraid of porting kung-fu movie choreography directly, study other forms of action or different media that evoke the action feeling. This reduces risk of visible porting while still achieving the intended energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your research up front, then stop refreshing the well
rubrics_metrics.description: Do all of your initial research ahead of time (read/watch similar works before you start), then let it settle instead of continually consuming the same sources while you write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Megan's approach: read two or three similar books or watch a few similar movies before starting. After initial research, avoid further close consumption to prevent mimicry ('eat jam on toast instead of going to pick more strawberries').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mentor texts to learn principles, not to follow instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentor texts are useful, but there's a point where following instructions without understanding the why becomes unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't copy a mentor's surface techniques blindly; extract the underlying principles so you can apply them in ways that suit your voice and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice via repetition / build muscle memory (simulate performers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like dancers or musicians, writers can simulate practice by repeatedly studying or performing elements to build 'muscle memory' for craft moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you need a specific scene type (e.g., love scene), consume examples to get into that headspace, then practice producing variations until it becomes natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform influences through processing (jam metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn strawberries into jam — process inspiration until it becomes something new rather than a straight copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boil/stew ideas: iterate, remix, and apply your skills so the output retains flavor of the influence but is a distinct creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely on a single similar source — diversify to avoid stealing specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: If your head is filled with only one similar work, you're more likely to port visible pieces; instead, fill it with many related works so they 'stew' together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consume a broad set of similar works (10–30) so direct borrowing is diluted and your own combinations are more likely to be original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let influences settle before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: After researching and consuming inspirations, let them settle in your mind before producing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow time for subconscious processing rather than immediate emulation; this helps you internalize principles instead of copying form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go deeper / extrapolate and extend the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore aspects of a work's systems or world that haven't been fully answered — going deeper can be especially satisfying and inspirational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: expand a magic system by asking previously unasked questions (how waterbending applies to blood). Use extension to find novel angles fans will love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about likes/dislikes to guide implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: When dissecting influence, note both what you like and what you don't, so you can intentionally adopt or reject elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this clarity to plan targeted practice and to avoid mindless imitation; decide what principles to import and which surface traits to avoid.
